title: Testing a Food-Waste Collection Proposal
description: Evaluate source credibility for specific claims and analyze how a writer acknowledges and responds to counterarguments.
subject: rla
author: Chee Skool
reviewNotes: Focused Arguments practice reviewed for one-best-answer logic, evidence fidelity, close distractors, and source-faithful explanations.

questions.prompt: Why is the city sanitation department a relatively strong source for the claim about how much residential waste is food scraps?

options.text: It is a government department, so everything it reports must be correct.
options.whyWrong: Institutional status alone does not guarantee accuracy; the stronger reason is its direct measurement of local waste.

options.text: It sampled Cedar Point household trash directly using a waste audit connected to the claim being evaluated.
It supports Brooks's preferred policy.
options.whyWrong: A source is not credible simply because it agrees with a position.

options.text: It has more employees than the regional composting facility.
options.whyWrong: Staff size does not determine whether the source is well positioned to measure household waste composition.

explanation.whyCorrect: The department has direct access to the relevant local material and used a measurement process tied to the claim.
explanation.quickTip: Judge credibility by expertise, access, method, and fit with the specific claim - not by whether you like the conclusion.

questions.prompt: What makes the regional composting facility a useful source for the capacity claim?

options.text: The facility is directly responsible for deciding how much material it can accept.
The facility is located outside Cedar Point.
options.whyWrong: Being regional does not by itself make the capacity statement more reliable.

options.text: The facility has probably handled every type of waste before.
options.whyWrong: The passage does not make this broad claim.

options.text: Its statement proves the pilot will reduce city costs.
options.whyWrong: Capacity evidence does not establish the financial effect of the program.

explanation.whyCorrect: The facility has direct operational knowledge of its own available capacity, making it well placed to address that specific question.
explanation.quickTip: A source can be highly credible for one claim and irrelevant to another.

questions.prompt: How does Brooks treat Reed's odor objection?

options.text: She dismisses it because restaurant owners have no relevant experience.
options.whyWrong: Brooks explicitly says his food-handling experience is relevant.

options.text: She accepts that odor makes any collection program impossible.
options.whyWrong: She acknowledges risk but offers evidence that design can reduce it.

options.text: She acknowledges the concern, limits how far Reed's restaurant experience can be generalized, and answers it with evidence from a similar household program.
She changes the subject from odor to road repairs.
options.whyWrong: The road-repair objection comes later; Brooks first responds directly to odor.

explanation.whyCorrect: A strong response can concede a legitimate concern without accepting the opponent's entire conclusion.
explanation.quickTip: Look for three parts: acknowledgment, limitation of the opposing evidence, and a direct response.

questions.prompt: Which source is MOST directly relevant to whether sealed household bins can keep odor complaints manageable over time?

options.text: Reed's twenty years running a restaurant kitchen.
options.whyWrong: His experience makes odor concerns plausible, but restaurant waste handling differs from the proposed household system.

options.text: The sanitation department's four-week waste audit.
options.whyWrong: The audit measures waste composition, not odor performance.

options.text: The composting facility's capacity letter.
options.whyWrong: Capacity does not address household odor complaints.

options.text: The two-year report from a nearby city using similar sealed bins and tracking complaints.

explanation.whyCorrect: The nearby-city report studies a closely comparable program and directly measures the outcome in question over time.
explanation.quickTip: Choose the source whose experience, method, and measured outcome best match the claim.

questions.prompt: Why does Brooks say the nearby-city report does NOT prove Cedar Point will get the same result?

options.text: A comparable source can inform the decision, but local conditions and implementation may differ.
Reports from other cities are never useful evidence.
options.whyWrong: Brooks uses the report precisely because it is relevant, while limiting the certainty of the comparison.

options.text: Odor complaints cannot be measured objectively.
options.whyWrong: The cited city tracked complaint rates over two summers.

options.text: Cedar Point has no sealed bins available.
options.whyWrong: The passage gives no such limitation.

explanation.whyCorrect: Similarity strengthens transfer, but evidence from another location still cannot guarantee identical local outcomes.
explanation.quickTip: Credible comparison evidence can support a prediction without turning it into certainty.

questions.prompt: What is the function of Brooks's response to the road-repair objection?

options.text: She argues that road repairs are unnecessary.
options.whyWrong: She does not deny the competing need.

options.text: She acknowledges the opportunity-cost concern and limits the pilot with a fixed budget and a new vote before permanent expansion.
She proves the pilot will cost less than road repairs.
options.whyWrong: No cost comparison is given.

options.text: She claims residents care more about compost than roads.
options.whyWrong: No preference data are provided.

explanation.whyCorrect: Her response addresses the concern by limiting financial exposure and requiring evidence before a permanent commitment.
explanation.quickTip: A counterargument response is stronger when it answers the actual objection rather than attacking a weaker version.

questions.prompt: Which statement best evaluates Reed as a source?

options.text: He is completely unreliable because he opposes the proposal.
options.whyWrong: Disagreement does not erase relevant experience.

options.text: He is the strongest source on citywide household complaint rates because he has run one restaurant for twenty years.
options.whyWrong: His experience is relevant to food handling but does not directly measure household collection outcomes citywide.

options.text: His experience makes the odor concern worth considering, but it is less directly matched to the proposed household system than data from a similar municipal program.
His opinion is stronger than measured evidence because practical experience always outweighs data.
options.whyWrong: Practical experience can matter, but “always” ignores fit, method, and scope.

explanation.whyCorrect: Credibility is claim-specific: Reed has relevant experience, but the nearby municipal program is a closer source for the exact policy design.
explanation.quickTip: Avoid all-or-nothing credibility judgments; ask how well the source is positioned for this particular claim.

questions.prompt: Which feature most strengthens Brooks's overall argument?

options.text: She never mentions any weakness in her proposal.
options.whyWrong: She discusses odor, cost, and uncertainty.

options.text: She treats every opposing claim as equally strong.
options.whyWrong: She distinguishes relevant concerns from conclusions that exceed the evidence.

options.text: She promises the pilot will succeed before it begins.
options.whyWrong: She frames the pilot as a way to test concerns.

options.text: She uses local and comparable evidence, acknowledges reasonable objections, and proposes a limited test that can generate new evidence.

explanation.whyCorrect: The argument combines evidence with a proportionate response to uncertainty instead of pretending the policy has no risks.
explanation.quickTip: Strong argumentation often improves when a writer addresses the best opposing point and shows how it can be tested.

curriculum.learningObjective: Evaluate source credibility for specific claims and analyze how a writer acknowledges and responds to counterarguments.
